a: Setting up accounts and deciding what each user is allowed to do
tasks.fb: Accounts, passwords, groups and permissions are all part of it.

tasks.q: Why does a shared computer need separate accounts?
a: So each user has their own files and settings, and can't reach anyone else's
tasks.fb: It's about privacy and protection, not performance.

tasks.q: Set the access each group needs on the school network.
tasks.fb: Least access that still lets each group do its job. Teachers read student work but shouldn't rewrite it.
tasks.note: Tip: a student must be able to change their own work; nobody but the network manager needs full control of everything.

tasks.q: Why is a student given read access to lesson resources, rather than read/write?
a: They need to open them, but must not be able to change or delete them
It stops the files being printed
tasks.fb: Least privilege: enough to work, no more.

tasks.q: What is the advantage of user groups?
a: One change to the group applies to every member at once
tasks.fb: Add a new teacher to the teachers group and they get the right access immediately.

tasks.q: A user signs in to a different computer and finds their own desktop and documents. What made that possible?
a: Their profile is stored on the network, not on one machine
tasks.fb: It's why any machine in the school feels like yours.

tasks.q: Put these in order, from the top of the hierarchy down to the file.
tasks.fb: That route, written out, is the file's path.

tasks.q: What does a file's path describe?
a: The route through the folders to reach that file
tasks.fb: Each folder name in the path is one step down the hierarchy.

stations.name: What the OS does with files

tasks.q: Which of these are file management jobs done by the operating system? Select all that apply.
opts: Moving a file to another folder
Recording where the file is stored on the disk
Deleting a file and freeing its space
Writing the contents of the essay
correct: Moving a file to another folder
Recording where the file is stored on the disk
Deleting a file and freeing its space
tasks.fb: The application writes the contents; the OS looks after the file itself.

tasks.q: What happens to the disk space when a file is deleted?
a: The OS marks it as free so it can be reused
The file moves to another disk
tasks.fb: Which is also why deleted files can sometimes be recovered until the space is reused.

tasks.q: Match each extension to what it holds.
tasks.fb: The OS uses the extension to pick the right program.

tasks.q: A student renames report.docx to report.jpg. What happens?
a: The file is unchanged inside, but the OS now tries to open it with the wrong program
tasks.fb: The extension is a label, not a conversion.

stations.name: Final challenge: lock down the network

tasks.q: A school's shared drive. Give each group the least access that lets it work.
tasks.fb: Least privilege every time: enough access to do the job, and no more.

tasks.q: Is each job user management or file management?
items: Creating an account for a new teacher
Putting a student into the Year 11 group
Moving a file into another folder
Recording which blocks a file uses
Freeing space when a file is deleted
tasks.fb: Both are jobs of the operating system, and both happen constantly.

info.title: Least privilege
info.text: Security teams call this the principle of least privilege: give every account the smallest access that still lets the work happen. It limits the damage when an account is stolen.

info.title: Who did what
info.text: Operating systems keep logs of who signed in, and what they opened. It's how a school can find out who deleted a shared file.

info.title: The root
info.text: On Windows the top of a drive is C:\; on Linux and macOS it is simply /. Either way, everything else hangs below it.

info.title: Long names
info.text: Early systems allowed eight characters and a three-letter extension, which is why old files have names like REPORT01.DOC.

info.title: Hidden extensions
info.text: Many systems hide extensions by default, which attackers exploit: invoice.pdf.exe looks like invoice.pdf in the file list.

info.title: Deleted isn't gone
info.text: Deleting a file usually removes the entry, not the data. Proper deletion overwrites the blocks, which is why organisations wipe drives before disposal.
